days.imageCredit: Marines rush ashore from Coast Guard landing craft at Empress Augusta Bay, Bougainville, 1 November 1943. U.S. Coast Guard photo, NARA 26-G-3120, public domain.
days.post:
One hidden Japanese gun destroyed four landing craft at Cape Torokina. The surf did far worse.

Just after sunrise on 1 November 1943, almost 7,500 Marines of the 3rd Marine Division made a 5,000 yard run for 12 beaches on Bougainville. Heavy surf threw the boats onto the wrong beaches and smashed them into each other. By midmorning 64 LCVPs and 22 LCMs lay wrecked on the sand, and three beaches had to be abandoned.

The prize was ground for airfields. Rabaul, Japan's main base in the region, lay less than 250 miles away, and by January 1944 fighters and bombers were striking it from Bougainville.

Was this landing the moment Rabaul stopped being a threat?
replies: Only about 270 Japanese soldiers held the cape, firing from 25 hidden bunkers. Sgt. Robert A. Owens, 23, placed four Marines to cover two neighboring bunkers, then charged straight into the mouth of the 75mm gun. He went in through the fire port and drove the crew out the back. He was killed, and he received the Medal of Honor after his death.

Photos: Marines rush ashore from Coast Guard landing craft at Empress Augusta Bay, Bougainville, 1 November 1943. U.S. Coast Guard photo, NARA 26-G-3120, public domain. On the card: The first wave heads for the beach at Empress Augusta Bay, Bougainville, 1 November 1943. U.S. Coast Guard photo, NARA 26-G-3123, public domain.

Sources: Top of the Ladder, Capt. John C. Chapin, USMC History and Museums Division; Landings at Cape Torokina and Robert A. Owens, Wikipedia; Pacific Wrecks; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo taken from inside a landing craft: Marines in camouflage helmets crowd toward the open ramp while the first men splash ashore and run up a sandy beach toward the jungle, Bougainville, 1 November 1943.
facts: Landing began just after sunrise, 1 November 1943, at Cape Torokina on Empress Augusta Bay, Bougainville. Code name Operation Cherryblossom.
Almost 7,500 Marines of the 3rd Marine Division, many in Coast Guard steered boats, ran 5,000 yards to 12 beaches. First wave ashore 7:26 a.m., four minutes early.
Surf wrecked the boats: 64 LCVPs and 22 LCMs lay wrecked by midmorning, and three beaches were abandoned.
One 75mm gun in a log bunker destroyed four landing craft and damaged ten more.
Only about 270 Japanese held the cape, in 25 hidden bunkers.
Sgt. Robert A. Owens, 23, charged the 75mm gun through its fire port. Killed, Medal of Honor.
24 war dogs landed too, mostly Doberman pinschers. About 14,000 men and 6,000 tons of supplies were ashore by nightfall.
Goal: airfields within 250 miles of Rabaul. Corsairs flew from Torokina from 10 December 1943.

days.title: Marines storm Cape Torokina

days.imageCredit: A Priest self propelled gun of the British 1st Armoured Division in the Western Desert, 2 November 1942. IWM E 18869, public domain.
days.post:
Brigadier John Currie warned that his tank brigade could lose half its strength. The answer: Montgomery had "accepted the possibility of losing 100% casualties" to make the break.

At 1:05 a.m. on 2 November 1942, Operation Supercharge opened at El Alamein. British infantry, joined by the New Zealand 28th (Maori) Battalion, moved off behind a creeping barrage from about 360 guns and took their objectives before dawn.

At 6:15 a.m. Currie's 9th Armoured Brigade charged the German and Italian antitank guns with the rising sun behind it. It started with 94 tanks. Fewer than 25 were still running at the end, and the gap did not open. That night, Rommel decided to fall back.

Was sending the 9th Armoured in a necessary sacrifice or a waste of brave men?
replies: Rommel then threw his panzers and the Italian Littorio Division at the British 1st Armoured Division near Tel el Aqqaqir. The counterattack failed, and the Afrika Korps lost about 70 tanks that day. That night its commander reported he would have at most 35 tanks the next morning.

Photos: A Priest self propelled gun of the British 1st Armoured Division in the Western Desert, 2 November 1942. IWM E 18869, public domain. On the card: Soldiers look over a knocked out German 88 mm gun near Tel el Aqqaqir, El Alamein, November 1942. Australian War Memorial 040977, public domain.

Sources: Second Battle of El Alamein and John Cecil Currie, Wikipedia; NZHistory; 51st Highland Division online museum; Arthur D. Simons Center.
days.alt: Archival photo of a British Priest self propelled gun, a tracked vehicle with a short gun barrel, stopped on flat open desert while its crew load gear onto it, November 1942.
facts: Supercharge opened at 1:05 a.m., 2 November 1942, Montgomery's final push to break Rommel's line at El Alamein.
Run by Freyberg's 2nd New Zealand Division, but most assault infantry were British: the 151st (Durham) and 152nd (Highland) Brigades, with the 28th (Maori) Battalion.
Creeping barrage from about 360 guns. The infantry reached their objectives before dawn.
9th Armoured Brigade under Brig. John Currie charged the antitank gun screen at 6:15 a.m., half an hour late, with the sun behind it.
Montgomery had "accepted the possibility of losing 100% casualties."
94 tanks at the start, fewer than 25 running at the end, 230 men killed, wounded or missing.
Currie, pointing to a handful of tanks: "These are my regiments."
The Afrika Korps lost about 70 tanks that day. That night Rommel decided to fall back to Fuka.

days.title: Supercharge breaks Rommel

days.imageCredit: Still from the U.S. Army film Japanese Paper Balloon (111-ADC-9990, NARA 23754), dated 1946: a serviceman examines the ballast ring of a captured balloon, hung with sandbags. Public domain.
days.post:
Japan never learned whether its balloon bombs worked. The United States made sure of that.

Before dawn on 3 November 1944, the Imperial Japanese Army launched its first Fu-Go balloons from the Pacific coast of Honshu. Paper balloons filled with hydrogen were meant to ride the winter jet stream more than 5,000 miles to North America, dropping sandbags at night to stay aloft, then dropping their bombs.

More than 9,000 were launched. Only about 300 were found or seen, from Alaska and Canada to Mexico and as far east as Michigan. On 4 January 1945 the Office of Censorship asked newspapers and radio not to report them. Japan stopped in April, with no news of any results.

The silence lasted until 22 May 1945, after a balloon bomb near Bly, Oregon, had killed a pregnant woman and five children.
replies: On 5 May 1945, on Gearhart Mountain near Bly, a church picnic group found a grounded balloon. Its bomb killed Elsie Mitchell, 26, and five children: Dick Patzke, 14, Joan Patzke, 13, Jay Gifford, 13, Edward Engen, 13, and Sherman Shoemaker, 11. They were the only people killed by enemy action in the continental United States during the war.

Photos: Still from the U.S. Army film Japanese Paper Balloon (111-ADC-9990, NARA 23754), dated 1946: a serviceman examines the ballast ring of a captured balloon, hung with sandbags. Public domain. On the card: A captured Japanese balloon bomb reinflated at NAS Moffett Field, California, 24 May 1945. U.S. Navy photo, NARA 80-G-326352, public domain.

Sources: Fu-Go balloon bomb, Wikipedia; Pacific Wrecks; Atomic Heritage Foundation; Smithsonian Magazine; Robert C. Mikesh, Smithsonian Annals of Flight No. 9; National Archives.
days.alt: Black and white film still of a serviceman in a cap reaching up to a captured Japanese balloon's metal ballast ring, hung with rows of small cloth sandbags and two long cylinders, over a plowed field.
facts: First Fu-Go launch before dawn, 3 November 1944, the birthday of the late Emperor Meiji.
Three launch sites on Honshu's Pacific coast: Otsu, Ichinomiya and Nakoso. About 200 balloons a day possible.
Hydrogen balloons of kozo mulberry paper glued with konnyaku paste, riding the jet stream about 30,000 feet up, 5,000 miles in a few days.
A barometer fired charges to drop sandbags at night. When the ballast ran out, the ring dropped the bombs: typically one 15 kg antipersonnel bomb and four incendiaries.
The Navy found one off California on 4 November 1944, the day after the first launch.
More than 9,000 launched by April 1945. About 300 found or seen in North America.
4 January 1945: the Office of Censorship asked the press not to report them. Made public 22 May 1945.
5 May 1945, near Bly, Oregon: six killed, the only deaths from enemy action in the continental U.S.

days.title: Paper bombs ride the jet stream

days.imageCredit: Lt. Gen. Bernard Montgomery in the turret of his Grant command tank at El Alamein, 5 November 1942. IWM E 18980, public domain.
days.post:
For more than two years, Britain's church bells stayed silent, saved as the alarm for a German invasion. On Sunday 15 November 1942, they rang across the country.

The reason was El Alamein. On 4 November 1942 the British broke through, and by early afternoon there was a 19 kilometre hole in Rommel's front. By his own figures he was down to 36 German tanks, from 249. At 5:30 p.m. he ordered a general retreat without waiting for Hitler's reply. About 30,000 Axis soldiers were taken prisoner in the battle.

Four days later, Operation Torch landed American and British troops in French North Africa, behind him. Which really doomed the Axis in Africa: Alamein or Torch?
replies: The same day, General Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma, commander of the Afrika Korps, surrendered to men of the 10th Hussars. Montgomery met him and later invited him to dinner. On 10 November Churchill told the Mansion House: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning."

Photos: Lt. Gen. Bernard Montgomery in the turret of his Grant command tank at El Alamein, 5 November 1942. IWM E 18980, public domain. On the card: Montgomery with the captured General von Thoma, El Alamein, 4 November 1942. No 1 Army Film and Photographic Unit, IWM E 19130, public domain.

Sources: Second Battle of El Alamein, Wikipedia; Rommel on his Defeat in Africa, German History in Documents and Images; National Army Museum; International Churchill Society; Essex Record Office.
days.alt: Archival photo of General Montgomery in a black beret and sweater standing in the open turret of his tank, holding binoculars, while a soldier beside him looks through binoculars, desert sky behind them.
facts: 3 November 1942, 1:30 p.m.: Hitler ordered Rommel to yield not a yard, "victory or death." Rommel obeyed at first.
4 November: the British broke through. Rommel wrote of a 19 kilometre hole in his front and no reserves.
Rommel's figures: 36 German tanks left on 4 November, from 249 at the start.
Gen. von Thoma, Afrika Korps commander, surrendered to the 10th Hussars. Montgomery later invited him to dinner.
5:30 p.m., 4 November: Rommel ordered a general retreat without waiting for Hitler's reply.
Much Italian infantry was left behind. About 30,000 Axis prisoners in the battle.
Church bells rang across Britain on 15 November 1942, the first time most people had heard them in over two years.
Churchill, 10 November: "the end of the beginning." Torch landed on 8 November.

days.title: Rommel retreats from Alamein

days.imageCredit: Bomb splashes around the Japanese cruiser Nachi in Manila Bay, 5 November 1944. U.S. Navy photo, NARA 80-G-287018, public domain.
days.post:
In spring 1945, Navy divers made 296 dives on a sunken Japanese cruiser in Manila Bay. They brought up secret documents, radar gear, and maps of the Japanese defenses on Luzon.

She was Nachi, Vice Adm. Kiyohide Shima's flagship at Surigao Strait. On 5 November 1944, two weeks after Leyte Gulf, Task Force 38's carrier planes struck Luzon's airfields and Manila Bay to wreck the air power feeding kamikazes into the fight for Leyte. Nachi tried to flee the bay at high speed. Planes from Essex hit her first, and planes from Lexington finished her with bombs, rockets and torpedoes.

She broke into three pieces near Corregidor. About 807 of her crew were killed, and about 220 survived.
replies: That afternoon a burning Japanese plane carrying a bomb crashed into Lexington's island. Her crew had the major fires under control in about 20 minutes, and her gunners shot down another kamikaze diving at Ticonderoga. About 50 of Lexington's men were killed and more than 120 wounded, the worst single loss in her long career.

Photos: Bomb splashes around the Japanese cruiser Nachi in Manila Bay, 5 November 1944. U.S. Navy photo, NARA 80-G-287018, public domain. On the card: The Japanese cruiser Nachi under attack by U.S. carrier planes in Manila Bay, 5 November 1944. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-287019, public domain.

Sources: WW2DB; Combinedfleet.com; Japanese cruiser Nachi and USS Lexington (CV-16), Wikipedia; Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships; National Archives.
days.alt: Archival aerial photo of the cruiser Nachi carving a long curving white wake across dark water in Manila Bay, ringed by the large white splashes of near miss bombs.
facts: 5 and 6 November 1944, two weeks after Leyte Gulf: carrier strikes on Luzon airfields and Manila Bay shipping.
Task Force 38, under Vice Adm. John S. McCain since 30 October. The aim was to cut off planes, including kamikazes, feeding the Leyte fight.
The new carrier Ticonderoga flew her first strike that morning. Her cameraman's slate: "Manila, 11/5/44."
Nachi, Shima's flagship at Surigao Strait, fled at high speed. Essex planes hit her first, Lexington planes finished her.
She broke in three near Corregidor. About 807 killed, about 220 survived. Shima watched from ashore.
A kamikaze hit Lexington's island: about 50 killed, more than 120 wounded.
The carriers returned 13 and 14 November and sank the cruiser Kiso and four destroyers.
Spring 1945: divers from USS Chanticleer made 296 dives on Nachi and recovered documents, radar gear and maps of Luzon's defenses.

days.title: Carriers strike Manila Bay

days.imageCredit: USS Omaha alongside the disguised German blockade runner Odenwald, 6 November 1941, photographed from USS Somers. U.S. Navy photo NH 49935, public domain.
days.post:
America was not at war, so the captain needed a reason to board a German ship. A National Archives photo caption says he chose "suspicion of slave trading."

On 6 November 1941, USS Omaha and USS Somers met a freighter near the equator flying the American flag, with "Willmoto, Philadelphia" on her stern. She was the German blockade runner Odenwald, carrying about 3,857 metric tons of raw rubber from Japan. As the boarding party climbed aboard, scuttling charges went off in the stern. The Americans plugged the flooding and took her to Puerto Rico.

In 1947 a court paid the sailors, but as salvage for saving an abandoned ship, not as prize money. Was this a lawful capture, or piracy with good paperwork?
replies: Each man in the boarding party received $3,000, and every other man on Omaha and Somers got two months' pay and allowances. The government took the rubber for the war effort on 24 December 1941. After Germany declared war, Odenwald was renamed Blenheim and carried cargo for the United States until 1945.

Photos: USS Omaha alongside the disguised German blockade runner Odenwald, 6 November 1941, photographed from USS Somers. U.S. Navy photo NH 49935, public domain. On the card: USS Omaha's prize crew aboard the captured German blockade runner Odenwald, 18 November 1941. U.S. Navy photo, NARA 80-G-464023, public domain.

Sources: Office of Naval Intelligence report on the M.S. Odenwald, uboatarchive.net; USS Omaha (CL-4), Wikipedia; National Archives; Hamburg American Line v. United States (1st Cir. 1948); NavSource.
days.alt: Archival photo of two ships far out on a calm open sea under a cloudy sky: the freighter Odenwald on the left and the cruiser USS Omaha on the right.
facts: 6 November 1941, a month and a day before Pearl Harbor, near the equator between Brazil and Africa.
Odenwald flew the U.S. flag, with "Willmoto, Philadelphia" painted on her hull and stern.
German motorship of the Hamburg America Line, out of Yokohama on 21 August 1941.
Cargo: about 3,857 metric tons of raw rubber, about 6,200 tons in all.
Capt. Theodore E. Chandler of Omaha sent an armed boarding party. Scuttling charges went off as they came aboard.
A NARA caption says he boarded on "suspicion of slave trading."
Reached San Juan, Puerto Rico, 17 November 1941.
1947 ruling: $3,000 per boarding party man, granted as salvage. Often called the Navy's last prize money.

days.title: The ship that lied

days.imageCredit: Still from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2651 (NARA 16455): soldiers of the 95th Signal Company cheer around a jeep carrying a Roosevelt Elected sign, Moyeuvre, France, 8 November 1944. Public domain.
days.post:
The day after Roosevelt won a fourth term, GIs in France paraded behind a jeep with a sign: Roosevelt Elected. The Army's own film notes called their joy "very stagey."

On 7 November 1944, in the middle of the war, Franklin D. Roosevelt beat Thomas E. Dewey, 432 electoral votes to 99. It was the closest of his four races, about 53.4 percent to 45.9, and millions of service members voted by absentee ballot.

His serious health problems were kept from the public. To answer the whispers, he toured New York City for four hours in an open car in pouring rain. Less than three months after his fourth inauguration, he was dead.

Should voters have been told how sick he was?
replies: His running mate was new. Party leaders turned against Vice President Henry A. Wallace, and Senator Harry S. Truman of Missouri took his place. Roosevelt died at Warm Springs, Georgia, on 12 April 1945, and Truman became president. The 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951, now limits presidents to two elected terms.

Photos: Still from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2651 (NARA 16455): soldiers of the 95th Signal Company cheer around a jeep carrying a Roosevelt Elected sign, Moyeuvre, France, 8 November 1944. Public domain. On the card: Roosevelt rides with Harry S. Truman and Henry Wallace after his reelection, Washington, 10 November 1944. Abbie Rowe, National Park Service, NARA 59-961, public domain.

Sources: The American Presidency Project; 1944 United States presidential election, Wikipedia; The National WWII Museum; National Archives; National Constitution Center.
days.alt: Black and white film still of American soldiers in helmets crowding around a jeep, some raising their arms and helmets in cheers, under a hand painted sign reading Roosevelt Elected.
facts: 7 November 1944: Roosevelt beat Dewey, 432 electoral votes to 99, carrying 36 of 48 states.
Popular vote about 25.6 million to 22.0 million, 53.4 to 45.9 percent, his closest of four.
New running mate: Sen. Harry S. Truman, after party leaders turned against Henry A. Wallace.
His health problems were kept from the public. On 21 October he toured New York City for four hours in an open car in pouring rain.
Millions of service members voted by absentee ballot.
8 November film from Moyeuvre, France: the 95th Signal Company parades behind a Roosevelt Elected jeep. Army notes: "very stagey."
Sworn in 20 January 1945 on the White House South Portico. Died 12 April 1945 at Warm Springs.
The only president elected four times. The 22nd Amendment (1951) limits presidents to two elected terms.
